At its core, the Pact for the Future is an affirmation of our shared responsibility to future generations. Critical minerals beneficiation at source in the African continent can play a key role of industrializing our continent and harnessing the energy of our young people. The ambitions of the Pact for the Future, including our commitment to youth, cannot be realized without adequate financing for development. To achieve the SDGs by 2030, Africa needs to close the annual financing gap of 1.3 trillion US dollars. Countries of the Global South face increased pressure on public finance, high borrowing costs, and the growing climate-related financial needs. Strengthening our capacity to mobilize resources for development is essential to developing on the priorities contained in the Pact of the Future. I thank you.

Thank you very much, Madam President, Excellencies. I am very pleased to join you for this high-level side event. We were very pleased to have co-facilitated the Declaration on Future Generations alongside the Kingdom of the Netherlands, and we continue to play a leadership role in advocating for its implementation post-adoption. The DFG holds special relevance for Africa, not only because of its transformational potential, but also because the concept of intergenerational fairness and equity is deeply rooted in traditional African knowledge systems. The idea that current generations bear a responsibility to those not yet born is therefore not unprecedented. Rather, it finds renewed importance and focus in the milestone consensual adoption of the DFG. The declaration provides a clear, concise and actionable framework for embedding futures thinking into all levels of decision making. By adopting the DFG by consensus, member states committed to using strategic foresight, data, statistics and science to improve policy making and invest in capacity to better prepare for and respond to global shocks and crises. It covers a wide range of persistent challenges. that are especially relevant for developing countries, including peace and security, migration, demographic shifts, harnessing the benefits of new and emerging technologies, strengthening resilient health systems, eradicating poverty, and advancing sustainable development. Jamaica's advocacy around the DFG stems from our belief in the immense potential it holds in driving positive change. As a practical way to advance this agenda, we established a group of friends for future generations last year, which we co-chair with the Kingdom of the Netherlands. This Group of Friends serves as a platform for Member States, futures practitioners, civil society partners, academia, and other like-minded stakeholders to share knowledge and best practices regarding implementation of the declaration. It maintains a cross-regional core group of Member States, including Kenya and several African nations. A number of countries across the continent are making leaps in DFG implementation. Kenya's Senate Futures Caucus is but one example of how long-term policymaking can be put into practice and adapted to address the most pressing needs of individual countries. The African Union's Agenda 2063 also shares alignment with several of the DFG's benchmarks, including on debt sustainability, youth employment and empowerment, and climate resilience. Africa, therefore, has a critical opportunity to demonstrate in real and practical terms the true value of the DFG in advancing the long-term ambitions. In closing, Madam President, I leave you with a well-known African proverb: "We do not inherit the Earth from our ancestors, we borrow it from our children." Let us continue to work together to ensure that those who follow us will be better off than we are today. I thank you.
